opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea starts from the scaling laws work, especially the Chinchilla paper. That gave us a recipe for being "compute optimal": if you have a fixed training budget, how should you split it between making the model bigger and training it on more data? Chinchilla's answer was roughly that you should scale both together, something like twenty tokens per parameter.

But that framing only optimizes for training compute, and training is just one part of the cost of actually deploying a model. Once you've trained it, you serve it to potentially millions of users, and every query costs inference compute that scales with the model's size. A larger model is more expensive to run, every single time someone uses it.

So if you expect heavy usage, the economics change. You might deliberately train a smaller model for much longer than Chinchilla would recommend, way past twenty tokens per parameter, sometimes hundreds or even thousands. Per unit of training compute, that's less efficient: you're spending extra to squeeze more performance out of a small model. But you get a model that's cheaper to serve at a given capability level, and if inference volume is large enough, the savings swamp the extra training cost.

That's essentially what we've seen with models like the Llama series and many of the smaller frontier-lab offerings. They're heavily "overtrained" relative to Chinchilla, and that's a rational response to the fact that lifetime inference spending can rival or exceed training spending.

There are some interesting implications. First, it means the training compute of a model isn't a clean indicator of its capabilities, since labs are trading off along this frontier. Second, it ties model design to market expectations: how many users you expect, how long the model will be in service before it's replaced. Third, there are limits. You eventually run into data constraints, because overtraining eats tokens fast, and returns diminish as you push a small model further. So it isn't a free lunch, but it's a big part of why capable, cheap models have proliferated so quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says heavy expected usage can make smaller models economical, but it does not attribute labs’ missed inference-cost savings to underestimating demand.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes spending more training compute to overtrain a smaller model in exchange for lower per-query inference costs.

r003.rationale: It links smaller frontier offerings to the lower serving costs that matter when a model is used by millions of people.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the starting point is the Chinchilla result from DeepMind, which told us that if you want to minimize training loss for a fixed training compute budget, there's an optimal way to split that budget between model size and the amount of data you train on. Roughly, you should scale parameters and tokens in equal proportion, so about twenty tokens per parameter.

But that framing only optimizes training compute. It ignores what happens after training. And for most labs, inference is where a very large share of the total compute actually goes. If you're going to deploy a model and serve it to millions of users, every query costs compute proportional to the model's size. So the real objective isn't "minimize loss per unit of training compute," it's something closer to "minimize total cost, training plus inference, for a given level of capability."

Once you include inference in the objective, the optimum shifts. A smaller model trained on far more data than Chinchilla would recommend can reach the same loss as a larger, Chinchilla-optimal model. You pay more in training, because you're pushing the model past the point of diminishing returns on data. But you get a model that's cheaper to serve on every single query for the rest of its deployment life. And if you expect to serve a lot of queries, that trade is overwhelmingly worth it.

So the economic logic is really a question of amortization. Training is a one-time fixed cost; inference is a recurring variable cost that scales with demand. The more demand you expect, the more you should front-load spending into training to shrink the per-query cost. That's why we've seen models like Llama trained on hundreds or even thousands of tokens per parameter, way beyond twenty.

There's also a point about hardware and latency. Smaller models fit on fewer accelerators, have lower memory requirements, and respond faster, which matters for product quality, not just for cost. And there's a strategic dimension: if you're releasing open weights, the people downstream will be the ones paying inference costs, so a model that's cheap to run is more useful to them and more widely adopted.

The one caveat I'd add is that this all depends on the expected inference volume. If you're doing a research run that you'll never deploy, Chinchilla-optimal is still the right target. Overtraining only makes sense when you're confident that inference demand will be large enough to pay back the extra training spend. But for frontier labs today, that's almost always the case.

r001.rationale: The response says high expected inference demand makes overtraining worthwhile, but it does not attribute labs’ missed chances to cut inference costs to underestimating that demand.

r002.rationale: It explains that overtraining raises training costs while enabling a smaller model with lower recurring inference costs.

r003.rationale: It links serving large numbers of users to the value of smaller, cheaper-to-serve models, explaining the shift toward overtraining them.

astra-6.text:
The key tradeoff is between the cost of training a model and the cost of using it. If you’re trying to get the best performance for a fixed training budget, there’s some optimal balance between the size of the model and the amount of data you train it on. But that doesn’t necessarily give you the model that’s cheapest to deploy.

You can instead train a smaller model on substantially more data. That might cost more upfront to reach a given level of capability, but the smaller model is cheaper to run each time someone uses it. That’s what “overtraining” means here: training beyond what would be optimal if you only cared about the training budget.

If the model is going to serve billions of requests, those savings at inference time can more than compensate for the additional training expense. So the economically optimal choice depends on how much demand you expect. The more heavily you expect a model to be used, the more it makes sense to spend upfront making a smaller model more capable.

r001.rationale: It says high expected demand can justify higher training costs, but does not attribute labs’ missed inference-cost savings to underestimating demand.

r002.rationale: It explains that training a smaller model on more data can cost more upfront while making each inference cheaper.

r003.rationale: It says heavy use can make a smaller capable model economically preferable, but does not attribute a trend toward smaller frontier models to serving very large numbers of users.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is between minimizing the cost of training a model and minimizing the total cost of training and using it. If you have a fixed training budget, there’s a balance between how big your model should be and how much data you should train it on. But that balance changes when you expect to serve the model to lots of users.

A smaller model is generally cheaper to run each time someone uses it. So it can make sense to train that smaller model on much more data, spending more upfront to get it to a given level of capability, because you then save money on every subsequent inference. If you’re going to run it billions of times, those savings can more than compensate for the additional training expense.

So “overtraining” is relative to a training-only notion of efficiency. From the perspective of the model’s entire lifetime, it can be the economically optimal thing to do. How far you should go depends on expected demand, inference costs, and how long the model will remain useful before it’s replaced.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expected demand and inference savings, but does not say labs missed cost-reduction opportunities because they underestimated demand.

r002.rationale: It explains spending more upfront to train a smaller model on more data in exchange for lower per-use inference costs.

r003.rationale: It says smaller models can be economical when usage is high, but does not attribute a trend toward smaller frontier models to serving very large numbers of users.
